subject: design-technology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the '6 Rs' of sustainable design?
options: Reduce
Rebrand
Relocate
Restock
questions.explain: The 6 Rs are Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Refuse, Rethink and Repair, all aimed at lowering environmental impact.

questions.q: What does the FSC (Forest Stewardship Council) logo on a product indicate?
options: The timber comes from responsibly managed, sustainable forests
The product is fully recyclable
The product was made using renewable energy
The product is Fairtrade certified
questions.explain: FSC certification shows that wood has been sourced from forests managed sustainably to protect the environment.

questions.q: In the '6 Rs', what does 'Reduce' primarily encourage a designer to do?
options: Use fewer materials and less energy in a product
Sell the product at a lower price
Reduce the number of colours available
Shrink the packaging logo
questions.explain: 'Reduce' means minimising the resources and energy used, cutting waste and environmental impact.

questions.q: A product's 'carbon footprint' is best described as:
options: The total greenhouse gas emissions caused across its life cycle
The physical area a product occupies when stored
The amount of carbon fibre used in its construction
The colour of the product's packaging
questions.explain: A carbon footprint measures the greenhouse gases released during a product's manufacture, use and disposal.

questions.q: Which of these is a finite (non-renewable) resource?
options: Crude oil
Wind
Solar radiation
Tidal movement
questions.explain: Crude oil is a fossil fuel that cannot be replaced within a human timescale, making it a finite resource.

questions.q: Which of the following is a renewable source of energy?
options: Wind
Coal
Natural gas
Crude oil
questions.explain: Wind is renewable because it is naturally replenished, unlike the finite fossil fuels coal, gas and oil.

questions.q: What is the key difference between recycling and reusing a product?
options: Reusing uses the product again as it is, while recycling reprocesses its materials into something new
Recycling uses the product again as it is, while reusing reprocesses the materials
They mean exactly the same thing
Reusing always requires melting the material down
questions.explain: Reuse keeps the product in its current form, whereas recycling breaks materials down to make new items.

questions.q: A designer wants to reduce the environmental impact of a wooden chair. Which action best applies the principle of 'design for disassembly'?
options: Using screws and bolts so parts can be separated and recycled at end of life
Gluing all joints permanently for strength
Painting the chair with a durable gloss finish
Adding decorative carvings to the legs
questions.explain: Design for disassembly uses temporary fixings so components can be taken apart, repaired or recycled.

questions.q: A company wants to cut the 'product miles' of its furniture. Which change would achieve this?
options: Sourcing timber from a local supplier instead of importing it
Using a rarer imported hardwood for quality
Shipping components between three overseas factories
Increasing the amount of packaging
questions.explain: Sourcing locally reduces the distance materials travel, lowering transport emissions and product miles.

questions.q: What does Fairtrade certification aim to guarantee?
options: A fair, stable price and better working conditions for producers
The lowest possible retail price for consumers
That the product is made entirely by machines
That the product is fully biodegradable
questions.explain: Fairtrade ensures producers in developing countries receive fair pay and improved working conditions.

options: Designing a product with a deliberately limited useful lifespan
Planning the layout of a factory in advance
Designing products to last as long as possible
Recycling a product at the end of its life
questions.explain: Planned obsolescence deliberately limits a product's life so consumers must replace it, raising sales and waste.

questions.q: Which of the following is an ethical concern associated with manufacturing goods offshore in low-wage countries?
options: Workers may face poor pay and unsafe working conditions
Products always have a lower carbon footprint
It guarantees higher product quality
It always increases the retail price
questions.explain: Offshore manufacturing can raise ethical concerns about exploitation, low wages and unsafe factories.

questions.q: How might culture influence the design of a product?
options: Colours, symbols or forms may carry different meanings in different societies
Culture has no effect on how products are designed
It only affects the price of a product
It determines the melting point of the material
questions.explain: Designers must consider cultural meanings, as colours and symbols can be interpreted differently across societies.

questions.q: A clothing brand wants to market itself as ethical. Which action best supports this claim?
options: Ensuring its supply-chain workers are paid a fair living wage
Using the cheapest possible unregulated factories
Increasing planned obsolescence to boost sales
Removing all recycling information from labels
questions.explain: Paying fair wages throughout the supply chain is a genuine ethical practice, unlike exploitative alternatives.

options: A new technology or material leads to the development of new products
Consumer demand drives the creation of a new product
A product is promoted by advertising alone
Retailers reduce the price to sell stock quickly
questions.explain: Technology push occurs when advances in technology or materials create opportunities for new products.

options: Consumer demand or need drives the development of a new product
A newly invented material creates a new product
Products are pulled from shelves due to faults
A government regulation forces a design change
questions.explain: Market pull happens when customer needs or demand lead designers to develop a product to meet them.

questions.q: What is one economic impact of increased automation in manufacturing?
options: Reduced labour costs but potential loss of manual jobs
It always increases the number of factory workers
It removes the need for any quality control
It guarantees products are more sustainable
questions.explain: Automation can cut labour costs and speed production but may reduce the need for manual workers.

questions.q: How can CAD/CAM benefit a manufacturing business economically?
options: It improves accuracy and speeds up production, reducing waste and costs
It removes the need to test any prototypes
It always eliminates all electricity costs
It makes products biodegradable
questions.explain: CAD/CAM increases precision and production speed, cutting material waste and manufacturing costs.

questions.q: A company receives a sudden large order for thousands of identical items to be produced quickly. Which manufacturing approach is most economical?
options: Mass (high-volume) production
One-off bespoke production
Making each item by hand individually
Producing in batches of two
questions.explain: Mass production efficiently makes large numbers of identical items at low unit cost, suiting high demand.
